units.label: 跨文化场景构造与数据验证
units.description: 从Cultural Atlas和World Values Survey选取文化常识与价值偏好，人工构造包含社会背景、角色档案、社会目标和文化知识的跨文化场景，并对场景是否可能引发文化冲突进行人工质量检查。

units.label: Antagonist文化冲突生成
units.description: 由antagonist agent依据角色、文化知识和社会目标启动对话，主动提出可能与参与者文化常识或价值偏好冲突的内容，以制造可观察的跨文化冲突。

units.label: Protagonist多轮社会目标互动
units.description: 由protagonist agent扮演目标角色，在最多20轮对话内与另一角色互动、逐一完成社会目标，并对antagonist提出的文化冲突作出反应。

units.label: Cultural Awareness评分
units.description: 根据protagonist是否在未被直接提示时识别并解释与文化规范或期待不一致的陈述/行动，以0/1评分文化觉察。

units.label: Cultural Knowledge评分
units.description: 将文化知识拆为文化常识和文化价值偏好；判断模型是否在对话中明确提及与场景给定知识一致的具体内容，分别以0/1评分。

units.label: Cultural Behavior评分
units.description: 社会目标完成与文化价值对齐的组合评分；正文与附录对1/2分对调，保留冲突，不确认实际运行版本。

units.label: 人工标注与LLM judge一致性核验
units.description: 从模型生成的场景中抽取样本，由具有社会心理学背景的研究生双重标注四个评价维度，并以人工标注为参照评估GPT-4o judge的准确率。

units.label: 跨国家、文化群组与价值主题分析
units.description: 按国家、World Values Survey文化群组和十个价值主题汇总模型的文化知识、觉察和行为表现，比较模型在不同文化情境中的差异及知识—行为关系。

facts.statement: 作者把文化能力拆成Cultural Awareness、Cultural Knowledge和Cultural Behavior三个维度，研究模型能否在跨文化互动中识别文化冲突、调用文化知识并在完成社会目标的同时调整行为。

method_function.text: 用动态社会互动把文化知识的拥有与情境中的行为应用分开测量。

facts.statement: 每个场景同时规定Social Goal和需要避免的Cultural Conflict；文化能力被定义为追求社会目标并防止跨文化冲突的能力。

method_function.text: 把目标完成与文化冲突管理放在同一个互动单元中考察。

facts.statement: 正式方法链由场景构造、模型角色扮演、多轮互动、四类评分和人工—LLM judge对照组成；评分与验证复用同一批模拟互动，不自动增加独立行为实验分母。

method_function.text: 把共享场景、互动和评分步骤按方法关系拆成可交接单元。

facts.statement: 每个场景由社会背景、角色和文化知识组成；角色档案包含性别、年龄、国籍和职业，并为角色规定需要完成的社会目标。

method_function.text: 固定场景字段，使不同模型在同一跨文化情境中接受可比输入。

facts.statement: 文化常识来自Cultural Atlas，作者选取其中Etiquette和Dates of Significance两个类别。

method_function.text: 为场景提供与日常规范和重要日期有关的文化常识刺激。

facts.statement: 文化价值问题来自World Values Survey Wave 7 Version 6.0；作者从覆盖多个国家和价值主题的问卷中选择适合国家间比较的价值偏好问题。

method_function.text: 用跨文化心理学调查材料构造文化价值条件。

facts.statement: 正文称人工筛选24个WVS文化价值问题，并关联到超过80%受访者赞同该陈述的国家，以形成国家层面偏好材料；附录A.2称21题，而表4A实际列出20个Question_ID。保留三个口径，不把其中一个静默当作已确认的最终题库数量。

method_function.text: 用人类回答分布筛选出对国家文化偏好有区分度的题目。

facts.statement: 基于所选文化知识，作者手工构造3,060个跨文化场景，覆盖60个国家、六大洲；场景数据按大洲统计，并对社会目标引发文化冲突的可能性进行人工质量检查。

method_function.text: 建立大规模、跨国家且带有文化冲突结构的刺激集合。

facts.statement: Antagonist agent的作用是启动文化冲突，作为互动的主要发起者，根据文化知识和社会背景提出可能触发冲突的陈述。

method_function.text: 让冲突以结构化方式进入对话，而不是等待模型自行生成冲突。

facts.statement: Protagonist agent扮演场景中的目标角色，与另一角色互动并逐一完成社会目标；附录提示要求在20轮内完成目标并结束对话。

method_function.text: 把模型反应放入有目标、有轮数上限的多轮社会互动中。

facts.statement: 模拟流程有三个阶段：先由antagonist制造文化冲突，再询问protagonist是否具有相关文化常识/价值知识，最后引出文化行为选择并评分。

method_function.text: 用连续阶段把觉察、知识和行为的证据分开。

facts.statement: 第一阶段由antagonist提出基于文化知识的冲突，例如在荷兰国王节安排工作；该阶段检验protagonist是否能识别潜在文化冲突。

method_function.text: 在未直接给出答案的互动开端测量文化觉察。

facts.statement: 第二阶段追问前一互动是否存在文化不适切性。附录antagonist提示还规定条件分支：先可不直接提供文化知识，若对方仍未意识到不适切性则提供明确知识后继续追问。因此所有后续回答不能一概解释为未经提示的原有知识。

method_function.text: 将文化知识的回忆/表达与前一阶段的自发觉察区分。

facts.statement: 第三阶段由antagonist提出与该文化中的价值偏好相冲突的主张，要求protagonist在继续追求社会目标时处理价值冲突。

method_function.text: 把文化价值应用放进仍需完成社会目标的行为选择中。

facts.statement: 文化觉察为0/1评分。正文强调识别冲突；附录judge提示明确要求在没有提示时独立识别并解释文化差异，不能只凭提示后的识别给1分。该提示的输出字段却写Cultural Knowledge Level，是原模板标签不一致，不将其当作另一个知识测量。

method_function.text: 用二元分数记录模型是否自发识别不适切互动。

facts.statement: Cultural Knowledge分为Cultural Commonsense Knowledge和Cultural Value Preferences；如果模型明确说出与给定知识一致的具体内容，该子指标记1分，否则记0分。

method_function.text: 将文化常识和文化价值偏好分别作为可观察的知识输出。

facts.statement: 文化行为把社会目标完成与文化价值对齐组合为0–3分。两处均将两者满足记3、两者不满足记0，但中间分数相反：正文将只对齐而牺牲目标记2、只追求目标未顾文化记1；附录表11A将只完成目标记2、只对齐文化记1。当前PDF不能确认出版统计实际采用哪一版，必须保留冲突。

method_function.text: 把社会目标和文化适切行为组合为0—3的行为结果。

facts.statement: 实验评估多个模型家族，包括Phi、Mistral、Llama、Qwen和GPT系列；开源模型用vLLM部署，AutoGen管理互动和评估线程，Qwen3-8B/32B采用No-Think设置。

method_function.text: 在多个现成模型上运行相同场景和评分流程。

facts.statement: agent模型temperature设为1以鼓励响应多样性，judge模型temperature设为0以保持评估稳定。

method_function.text: 分别控制生成多样性和评分稳定性。

facts.statement: 人工验证随机抽450个模拟场景：LLaMA-3-70B为100，其余七模型各50。两名社会心理学背景研究生先接受书面指南与校准，再对所有样本双重标注；分歧与第一作者讨论解决，同一对标注员评所有维度。论文在所查验证段未报告裁决前一致性数值，不能把最终共同标签称为已量化的独立标注一致性。

method_function.text: 用有限人工样本检验自动评分的可用性。

facts.statement: 附录表5A报告GPT-4o judge相对人工标签的准确率：文化觉察88%、文化常识88%、文化价值92%、文化行为84%。正文笼统称accuracy exceeding 88%，与这些分维度结果不一致；不能据此称每个维度均超过88%。

method_function.text: 报告自动评分相对人工标注的维度级一致性/准确率。

facts.statement: 表2列14个模型的文化觉察、常识、价值、行为均分及0–3分等级百分比；图5标题说明8个模型在21个国家的觉察/知识比较，正文说明这21国按场景数量最多选取。总体模型表与子集国别分析的分母需分开，不能都称8个模型或完整60国分析。

method_function.text: 保留不同指标层级，避免把行为分数压缩成单一榜单。

facts.statement: 论文进一步按8个World Values Survey文化群组和10个价值主题分析模型的文化价值理解表现。

method_function.text: 把文化价值差异分解为文化群组和主题两个分析轴。

facts.statement: 论文报告模型拥有的文化知识与互动中的文化觉察/行为并不等价：GPT-4o在文化常识知识上较强，但应用知识避免冲突和适应文化价值方面仍有困难。

method_function.text: 直接比较知识、觉察和行为三个层级的脱钩。

facts.statement: 论文报告不同模型在文化群组和价值主题上的表现不均衡，例如在Confucian群组、英语文化群组或拉丁美洲社会政治议题上呈现不同的对齐模式。

method_function.text: 用情境分层展示模型行为不是跨文化均匀的。

facts.statement: 正文与图7统计“有文化觉察但未表现出相关明确文化知识”的回答，并按礼仪/重要日期类别展示数量；附录用代表案例说明这种分离。作者认为这些现象提示觉察与知识可区分；这不是已排除评分误差的构念独立性证明。

method_function.text: 保留“知道”与“意识到风险”之间的行为差异。

facts.statement: 作者将观察到的跨文化对齐差异与模型预训练中形成的文化偏差联系起来，并认为这些偏差会影响跨文化泛化和行为反应。

method_function.text: 记录作者解释，同时不把它当作已实施的偏差控制。

facts.statement: 论文未来方向包括用SocialCC做fine-tuning以提升文化能力；当前论文的方法和结果部分没有把该fine-tuning作为正式实验操纵。

method_function.text: 明确区分当前推理期评估与作者提出的未来训练方向。

facts.statement: 作者承认60国六大洲仍不能完整代表全球文化细节；Cultural Atlas与WVS是静态来源，文化规范会随全球化、迁移和社会变化而改变。

method_function.text: 把覆盖和知识时效性作为解释边界保留。

facts.statement: 该基准以英语设计以保持比较一致性，因此对非英语文化和语言资源有限地区的文化理解不能充分评估。

method_function.text: 标记语言覆盖对行为解释的限制。

facts.statement: 作者承认数据集和指标可能含有文化偏差，尽管通过多样化场景和社会科学专家支持进行缓解；仍可能被误用于强化刻板印象。

method_function.text: 把风险讨论记录为限制，不把它误写成已完成的控制实验。

facts.statement: 附录案例只展示典型模型互动及评分现象，用于说明觉察、知识和行为之间的差异；案例本身不构成独立实验分母。

method_function.text: 防止将示例对话误算为额外行为实验。

facts.statement: 模板输入存在信息差：antagonist获得文化常识/文化价值块，protagonist模板只有场景、事件、人物档案和社会目标，没有同样的知识块。该结论限于公开模板，不证明所有实际API请求均严格遵守，也不表示模型先验知识已被消除。

method_function.text: 区分冲突发起者与被测角色的已提供信息。

facts.statement: antagonist提示依据protagonist是否同意建议、是否给出文化理由、是否意识到不适切性选择追问；有的分支不直接提供知识，有的提供明确知识。双方模板要求20轮内完成目标，antagonist以Hello开始并以OK. GOOD BYE!结束，protagonist以GOOD BYE!结束。

method_function.text: 用条件追问与停止协议组织互动。

facts.statement: judge模板接收场景、文化知识和对话历史，按维度给出固定字段与离散分数；价值和行为提示明确判断Event 2。觉察要求未受提示，常识提示从历史中判断是否明确说出知识；模板没有完整规定逐轮截取和提供知识前后回答的隔离实现。

method_function.text: 按评分对象和事件范围把对话转为可核验标签。

evidence.quote: Cultural competence refers to the ability of individuals to interact appropriately with people from diverse cultural backgrounds (Earley and Ang, 2003). People demonstrate cultural competence by tailoring their behaviors to avoid cultural conflict during intercultural interaction (Chen and Starosta, 2012). It encompasses three fundamental subabilities: Cultural Awareness, which leverages cultural knowledge to detect inappropriate interactions; (Pawar et al., 2024), Cultural Knowledge, which refers to possessing cultural commonsense, values, and other knowledge; and Cultural Behavior,which is the ability to adapt appropriately in cross-cultural interactions(Sternberg, 2004).

To address these limitations, we introduce SocialCC, a novel framework for evaluating the cultural competence of language agents through interactive socio-cultural scenarios. Our framework features 3,060 carefully designed intercultural scenarios spanning 60 countries across six continents. Within these scenarios, LLM-driven agents engage in multi-turn interactions, navigating culturally challenging situations while pursuing specific social goals. The framework assesses agents’ cultural competence in three key dimensions: Cultural Awareness: the ability to leverage cultural knowledge to identify inappropriate interactions. Cultural Knowledge: possessing the cultural knowledge including cultural commonsense and cultural values, and Cultural Behavior: the ability to adapt its behavior appropriately to avoid cultural conflict while achieving social goals. Building on established research in sociology, we employ a comprehensive evaluation methodology using multi-dimensional criteria, assessed by both human judges and LLM-based judges. Our analysis highlights a significant gap between language models’ stored cultural knowledge and their ability to effectively apply it in intercultural social interactions. Furthermore, LLMs exhibit a limited understanding of cultural knowledge, particularly cultural values across different countries, and struggle to autonomously integrate these values into appropriate behavioral responses during social interactions.

SocialCC employs intercultural social scenarios in which large language models engage in roleplaying interactions to dynamically assess their cultural competence. By simulating real-world cross-cultural exchanges, this framework systematically evaluates how effectively LLMs apply cultural knowledge to mitigate potential cultural conflicts and achieve intended social goals. We propose an overall framework as shown in Figure 2. Intercultural Social Scenarios The core component of Social Duolingo is the diverse set of intercultural scenarios designed to structure and evaluate cross-cultural interactions between agents. Each scenario serves as a controlled environment for assessing cultural competence, where two key components are measured: (1) Social Goal is what the agent aims to achieve within an intercultural scenario, such as organizing a multinational conference or presenting a gift. The agent’s proactive engagement in social interactions is driven by this goal, shaping its participation in dynamic social exchanges. (2) Cultural Conflict is the challenges the agent must avoid while navigating intercultural interactions. Cultural conflicts arise when the agent’s responses fail to align with the cultural commonsense knowledge and values of the participants involved. The agent is expected to consciously recognize cultural discrepancies and take appropriate actions to prevent conflicts. In summary, an agent’s cultural competence is reflected in its ability to pursue social goals while effectively preventing cultural conflict in the intercultural interactions.

As shown in Figure 2, each scenario primarily consists of three main components: the social background, characters, and cultural knowledge. We first collect cultural knowledge and then manually construct intercultural scenarios, including character profiles that specific gender, age, nationality, and occupation. Additionally, we define the social goals the characters need to accomplish, which may lead to cultural conflicts.

Cultural Knowledge Selection We select the Cultural Atlas (Evason, 2019) as the source of cultural commonsense knowledge. As an authoritative cultural resource validated by community experts, the Cultural Atlas provides cultural commonsense knowledge across 12 categories spanning six continents. We focus on two of these categories: Etiquette and Dates of Significance.

We collect 24 cultural values questions from the World Values Survey (WVS) (Haerpfer et al., 2022), covering responses from 60 countries. The WVS project gathers responses to a wide range of value-based questions across 13 topics from demographically controlled population samples worldwide. Our benchmark includes 10 topics: Social Value, Migration, Corruption, Happiness, Social Capital, Economic, Religious, Ethical, and Political Interest, and Political Culture. The WVS is widely used as a dataset for computational modeling (Johnson et al., 2022; Kovač et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024a). Our benchmark is built upon the latest Wave 7 (Version 6.0) of the WVS, conducted between 2017 and 2022, covering over 129,000 respondents from 64 countries. The survey consists of 259 questions presented in a questionnaire format, including both multiple-choice and openended questions.

Not all value-based questions in the WVS are suitable for evaluating a language agent’s understanding of cultural value preferences in specific countries. Some questions reveal strong nationallevel preferences, while others show little variation across countries. As shown in Figure 3, responses to Question 28 “When a mother works for pay, the children suffer” exhibit strong agreement in some countries and show the cultural value preference. To ensure a meaningful evaluation, we select culturally skewed questions where human responses show strong consensus within specific countries. We manually curate 24 questions, each associated with countries where over 80% of respondents agreed with the statement. This selection process enables a assessment of LLMs’ cultural competence by evaluating their ability to align with culturally prevalent perspectives in individual countries.

Data Validation and Statistics Based on the selected cultural knowledge, we handcraft 3,060 intercultural scenarios covering 60 countries. We conduct the human validation to ensure the quality of our benchmark. For each scenario, we consider whether the social goal for agents has the potential to cause cultural conflict. 3.4 Evaluation Evaluating the cultural competence of language agents requires a structured assessment of their ability to recognize, understand, and appropriately respond to culturally sensitive interactions. To achieve this, we define three key dimensions: Cultural Awareness, Cultural Knowledge, and Cultural Behavior. Each dimension is assessed based on a specific set of criteria designed to quantify the agent’s cultural competence. Cultural Awareness refers to an agent’s ability to leverage cultural knowledge to identify inappropriate interactions in intercultural scenarios. This capability is demonstrated when the agent detect instances where a particular statement or action is misaligned with the cultural norms or expectations of other participants in an intercultural social scenario. Therefore, we assign a score of 1 if the agent successfully identifies a cultural conflict or inconsistency and a score of 0 if it fails to do so.

Cultural Knowledge pertains to the depth and breadth of an agent’s understanding of cultural norms, values, and social conventions. We categorize this knowledge into two components: (1) Cultural Commonsense Knowledge: widely shared knowledge about daily life and societal norms within a specific country. (2) Cultural Value Preferences: Deep-seated beliefs and ethical principles that shape behaviors and expectations within a particular cultural group. If the agent correctly identifies the specific commonsense knowledge or cultural value preference, we assign a score of 1;

Cultural Behavior evaluates the extent to which an agent’s responses align with social and cultural expectations in real-world interactions. This dimension is assessed based on two key factors: whether the agent successfully achieves the intended social goal (Social Goal Completion) and whether its response avoids cultural conflict (Cultural Conflict Management). An agent that successfully accomplishes its social goal while respecting others’ cultural norms demonstrates strong cultural behavior and receives a score of 3. If the agent prioritises respecting others’ cultural norms at the expense of its own task completion, it is awarded 2 points. 5.3 LLMs’ Performance Across Cultural Groups As shown in Figure 6, large language models demonstrate varying degrees of alignment with different cultural groups, in part due to their implicit associations with the value dimensions identified by the World Values Survey. For example, LLaMA3.1-70B and Qwen3-32B exhibit strong alignment with Confucian cultural groups, particularly in their interpretation of secular-rational values—such as an emphasis on education, individual effort, and national stability.

Beyond the Confucian group, GPT-4.1 shows relatively consistent alignment with English-speaking cultures, likely due to its recognition of the lower emphasis on religion and strong support for individual rights that characterise these societies. In this study, we introduce SocialCC, a benchmark designed to assess the cultural competence of LLMs through interactive, multi-turn scenarios. Our extensive dataset encompasses 3,060 humancrafted scenarios across 60 countries, providing a comprehensive platform to evaluate LLMs’ ability to navigate complex intercultural interactions. Our evaluation of models like GPT-4.1 and LLaMa370B reveal that, despite some cultural adaptability, significant challenges persist in accurately interpreting nuanced cultural contexts. These findings highlight the need for further research to enhance AI systems’ cultural intelligence, ensuring their effectiveness in global applications such as customer service and cross-cultural education. Future research directions include leveraging the SocialCC benchmark for fine-tuning LLMs to improve their cultural competence and exploring adaptive mechanisms that allow AI to modify its responses based on cultural cues dynamically. Additionally, expanding our dataset to include more diverse cultural scenarios will further enhance the robustness of evaluations. By advancing the cultural competence of AI, we move closer to developing systems that are not only intelligent but also culturally aware, fostering more meaningful and respectful human-AI interactions.

Static Cultural Knowledge Sources Our benchmark leverages well-established cultural knowledge bases, such as the Cultural Atlas and the World Values Survey, to ensure reliability and consistency. However, cultural norms are dynamic and continuously shaped by factors such as globalization, migration, and social change. Future iterations could explore incorporating real-time cultural insights and adaptive knowledge sources to better reflect evolving cultural landscapes. Multilingual Considerations As an initial step, our benchmark is designed in English to enable a standardized evaluation of models’ cultural competence across different regions. While this approach supports comparability, it may not fully address cultural understanding in non-English-speaking regions. For instance, in areas where local language resources are limited, such as Bangladesh, models with less exposure to these languages may face challenges in processing culturally nuanced questions. Expanding to multilingual settings in future work could help address these limitations and provide a more comprehensive assessment of cultural

Ethics Statement The dataset used in this study is publicly available and does not contain personally identifiable information. No human subjects were directly involved, and thus, no Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval was required. Our study examines the cultural competence of language agents, a topic that inherently involves biases related to cultural representation. We acknowledge that the dataset and evaluation metrics may contain cultural biases, and we have taken steps to mitigate these by diversifying test scenarios and incorporating research support from social science experts. However, biases may still persist, and we encourage future work to explore more robust fairness measures. Additionally, while our framework aims to enhance cross-cultural understanding, it could be misused to reinforce stereotypes if not properly applied. Equipped with social backgrounds, profiles, social tasks and cultural knowledge, it strategically introduces tensions and steers the conversation to challenge the cultural competence of the protagonist agent in respond appropriately. As the evaluated participant, the protagonist agent is given social backgrounds, profiles, and specific social goals, which guide its engagement in interactions. Its responses to the antagonist agent’s challenges reflect its ability to recognize cultural conflicts and take actions to resolve them effectively.

Simulation Pipeline As illustrated in Figure 4, the detailed simulation process consists of three key stages as follows: • Step 1: Cultural Conflict Generation The antagonist agent initiates an interaction by making a statement that, based on the given cultural knowledge and social backgrounds, is designed to trigger a cultural conflict. For example, as shown in Figure 4, the antagonist agent proposes scheduling a meeting on April 27th, a significant holiday in the Netherlands. This step evaluates whether the protagonist agent can detect the potential cultural conflict, thereby demonstrating its cultural awareness. It reflects the agent’s ability to recognise that the same content—such as a specific date—may carry different implications across countries; for instance, a date that is a regular workday in one country may be a national holiday in another. • Step 2: Cultural Knowledge Questioning The antagonist agent follows up by questioning whether the protagonist agent about potential cultural inappropriateness in the preceding interaction. This step evaluates whether protagonist agent possesses the fundamental cultural commonsense knowledge necessary to identify culture-related conflicts. • Step 3: Cultural Behavior Elicitation The antagonist agent then introduces a proposition that contradicts widely accepted cultural value preferences within a given culture and social scenario. For instance, in Figure4, the antagonist agent

proposes that everyone work overtime on April 27th, conflicting with the cultural value preference in the Netherlands, where leisure time is highly prioritized. This step evaluates whether the protagonist agent can identify value-based conflicts and take appropriate action to resolve the cultural conflict while still achieving its social goals. See Appendix C for Simulation Prompts.

Cultural Behavior evaluates the extent to which an agent’s responses align with social and cultural expectations in real-world interactions. This dimension is assessed based on two key factors: whether the agent successfully achieves the intended social goal (Social Goal Completion) and whether its response avoids cultural conflict (Cultural Conflict Management). An agent that successfully accomplishes its social goal while respecting others’ cultural norms demonstrates strong cultural behavior and receives a score of 3. If the agent prioritises respecting others’ cultural norms at the expense of its own task completion, it is awarded 2 points. However, if the agent pursues its goal while failing to consider others’ cultural expectations, it receives 1 point. Finally, if the agent fails to achieve its goal and causes cultural conflict, it is assigned a score of 0.

5.1 Cultural Knowledge vs. Cultural Awareness We select the 21 countries with the highest number of scenarios. Figure 5 shows the performance of LLMs in cultural awareness and cultural knowledge across these countries. As previous studies have found(Adilazuarda et al., 2024; Shen et al., 2024), LLMs exhibit English cultural dominance, and their cultural knowledge tends to be more extensive for cultures well-represented in the training data, such as Germany and China. However, possessing cultural knowledge does not necessarily equate to cultural awareness. For example, while LLMs demonstrate a high level of cultural knowledge in countries like the United States and Croatia, their cultural awareness remains limited. We analyze how LLaMa-3 series exhibits cultural awareness that extends beyond the limits of its cultural knowledge. As illustrated in Figure 7, we examine cases where LLMs demonstrate cultural awareness despite lacking relevant cultural knowledge. Notably, LLMs tend to show greater cultural awareness in etiquette scenarios. For instance, as discussed in case study D.2, while LLMs may not explicitly know that chrysanthemums symbolize mourning in the Netherlands, they recognize their association with death in China and avoid gifting them, demonstrating implicit awareness of cultural sensitivity. A higher level of cultural competence emerges when an LLM not only recognises that the same cultural symbol may carry different—or at times similar—meanings across countries, but also consciously infers and navigates potential cultural conflicts, even its cultural knowledge is limited.

(2) Survival values prioritize economic and physical security, whereas Self-expression values emphasize environmental protection and greater participation in social and political life. Based on these two dimensions, WVS categorizes countries into eight groups, as shown in Appendix A.3. Countries within the same group share similar cultural value preferences. Figure 6 shows the performance of different LLMs in interpreting the cultural value preferences within these eight clusters. During intercultural interactions, LLM agents exhibit a more accurate understanding of Confucian values, particularly by placing less importance on religion and authority and appropriately prioritizing environmental protection, LGBTQ+ rights, and gender equality. As a result, LLMs tend to interpret cultural values through a secular-rational lens, which limits their cultural competence in recognizing and respect traditional value preferences upheld by a broad range of countries. In addition to variation across cultural groups, LLMs also exhibit topic-specific biases when engaging with different cultural value domains. Among the ten value-related topics examined, their performance is uneven—showing relatively better comprehension of topics such as Economic, Corruption, and Political Culture, while consistently underperforming on others like Migration and Happiness. These topic-level disparities further constrain LLMs’ capacity to accurately interpret and apply cultural value preference in interactive contexts.

The LLaMa-3 and GPT series demonstrate some capabilities, but their overall performance remains suboptimal. As expected, GPT-4o outperforms other models in cultural commonsense knowledge. However, it struggles to apply this knowledge effectively in intercultural interactions. Due to its limited understanding of cultural value preferences across different countries, it fails to adapt its behavior effectively to prevent conflicts effectively. Several cases are presented in Appendix D.1. In contrast, GPT-4.1 and LLaMa3-70B, though not equipped with more cultural knowledge, display heightened sensitivity to cultural conflicts, reflecting stronger cultural awareness. They also demonstrate a better grasp of other participants’ cultural value preferences. By effectively integrating cultural awareness and knowledge to navigate social interactions—while respecting diverse value perspectives and achieving social goals— GPT-4.1 and LLaMa3-70B outperform other models in cultural behaviour.
